recall_items.stem: A column of ages has 4 percent missing values. The missingness is unrelated to anything else in the data. Which approach keeps the rest of each row and distorts the age distribution least?

options.A: Replace each missing age with 0.
options.B: Replace each missing age with the median age.
options.D: Replace each missing age with the maximum age.

recall_items.explanation: With missingness unrelated to other variables and a small share missing, median imputation keeps the rows and barely shifts the center of the distribution. It does shrink the spread slightly, which is the known cost.

misconceptions.A: Treats a missing value as a real age of zero, which creates fake infants.
misconceptions.C: Throws away 96 percent of the real values to handle 4 percent missing.
misconceptions.D: Fills with an extreme value and shifts the mean upward.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A revenue column loads as text because some cells contain '$1,200'. What is the right order of operations?

options.A: Convert to float first, then strip the symbols.
options.B: Strip '$' and ',' first, then convert to float.
options.C: Drop every row that contains a '$'.
options.D: Keep it as text and sort alphabetically.

recall_items.explanation: The symbols stop the type conversion, so they are removed first. Then the clean strings convert to numbers.

misconceptions.A: The conversion fails on '$1,200' before anything is stripped.
misconceptions.C: Deletes the rows with the most information about revenue.
misconceptions.D: Alphabetical order puts '9' after '10,000' and makes sums impossible.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A table of orders has 10,000 rows. After an inner join to a customers table keyed on customer_id, it has 12,400 rows. What most likely happened?

options.A: The join dropped orders with no matching customer.
options.B: Some customer_id values appear more than once in the customers table, so matching orders were duplicated.
options.C: pandas added rows to fill missing dates.
options.D: The orders table had hidden rows that the join revealed.

recall_items.explanation: An inner join can only lose rows or, when the key is not unique on the right side, multiply them. Growth from 10,000 to 12,400 means some customers matched more than once.

misconceptions.A: Dropping rows would lower the count, not raise it.
misconceptions.C: Joins never invent dates; row growth comes from duplicate keys.
misconceptions.D: A join exposes nothing hidden; it combines rows by key.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Which table layout is 'tidy' in the sense used in data analysis?

options.A: One row per city, one column per month, cells hold sales.
options.B: One row per city and month, with columns city, month, sales.
options.C: One row per sale with a free-text description column only.
options.D: One column that stores 'city-month-sales' as a single string.

recall_items.explanation: Tidy data has one variable per column and one observation per row. City, month and sales are each their own column, and each row is one city-month observation.

misconceptions.A: Months spread across columns are values stored as column names (wide format).
misconceptions.C: Free text mixes several variables into one cell.
misconceptions.D: Three variables are packed into one column.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Monthly revenue over three years. Which chart shows the trend best?

options.A: A pie chart with one slice per month.
options.B: A line chart with months on the x-axis.
options.C: A scatter plot of revenue against itself.
options.D: A bar chart sorted from highest to lowest month.

recall_items.explanation: A single quantity over evenly spaced time is a line chart. The eye reads slope and seasonality directly.

misconceptions.A: A pie shows parts of one whole, not change over time.
misconceptions.C: Plotting a variable against itself shows a diagonal and nothing else.
misconceptions.D: Sorting by value destroys the time order, so the trend disappears.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Household income has a mean of 85,000 and a median of 62,000. What does this suggest about the distribution?

options.A: It is symmetric.
options.B: It is skewed to the right, with a long tail of high incomes pulling the mean up.
options.C: It is skewed to the left, with a tail of low incomes.
options.D: The data must contain errors.

recall_items.explanation: When the mean sits well above the median, a minority of large values pulls the mean up. That is right skew, which is typical for income.

misconceptions.A: A symmetric distribution has mean and median close together.
misconceptions.C: Left skew would pull the mean below the median.
misconceptions.D: Mean above median is a normal feature of income data, not an error.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A bar chart compares two products' conversion rates: 3.1 percent and 3.4 percent. The y-axis starts at 3.0 percent. What is the problem?

options.A: Bar charts cannot show percentages.
options.B: The truncated axis makes a 0.3-point gap look like the second bar is four times taller.
options.C: Conversion rates should always use a log scale.
options.D: There is no problem; truncated axes are standard for bar charts.

recall_items.explanation: Bar length encodes value from zero. Starting the axis at 3.0 turns a 10 percent relative difference into a visual 4-to-1 ratio.

misconceptions.A: Bars show percentages fine when the axis starts at zero.
misconceptions.C: A log scale is for data that spans orders of magnitude, which this does not.
misconceptions.D: Truncated axes are standard for line charts of levels, not for bars.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: The middle 50 percent of a distribution lies between the first and third quartiles. The distance between them is called the ______.

options.A: standard deviation
options.B: interquartile range
options.D: confidence interval

recall_items.explanation: The interquartile range is Q3 minus Q1 and is the box in a box plot. It is robust to outliers.

misconceptions.A: The standard deviation measures spread around the mean, not between quartiles.
misconceptions.C: Variance is the squared standard deviation.
misconceptions.D: A confidence interval is about an estimate's uncertainty, not the data's spread.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A test for a condition is 99 percent sensitive and 95 percent specific. The condition affects 1 in 1,000 people. Someone tests positive. Roughly what is the chance they have the condition?

options.A: About 99 percent
options.B: About 95 percent
options.D: About 50 percent

recall_items.explanation: Per 100,000 people: 100 have it and 99 test positive; 99,900 do not and about 4,995 test positive anyway. Positive tests: 5,094, of which 99 are true. 99 / 5,094 is about 1.9 percent. Bayes' rule with a low base rate.

misconceptions.A: Confuses sensitivity, the chance of a positive given the condition, with the chance of the condition given a positive.
misconceptions.B: Reads specificity as the answer; it describes people without the condition.
misconceptions.D: Ignores the base rate of 1 in 1,000.

recall_items.author: hand

options.A: P(A)
options.B: P(B)

recall_items.explanation: Bayes' rule divides the joint probability P(B | A) P(A) by the marginal P(B), which normalizes it to a probability of A given B.

misconceptions.A: Dividing by P(A) cancels the prior and leaves P(B | A), the wrong direction.
misconceptions.C: The numerator already is P(A and B); dividing by it gives 1.
misconceptions.D: 1 - P(B) is the probability of not B and has no place in the rule.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Which distribution models the number of support tickets arriving in an hour, when tickets arrive independently at a steady average rate?

options.A: Normal
options.B: Poisson
options.D: Bernoulli

recall_items.explanation: Counts of independent events in a fixed interval at a constant rate follow a Poisson distribution.

misconceptions.A: The normal is continuous and allows negative values; counts are non-negative integers.
misconceptions.C: Uniform would make 0 tickets and 50 tickets equally likely.
misconceptions.D: Bernoulli is a single yes-or-no trial, not a count.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A lottery ticket costs $2 and pays out $100 with probability 0.01, otherwise nothing. What is the expected net gain per ticket?
recall_items.explanation: Expected payout is 0.01 times $100, which is $1. Subtract the $2 price and the expected net gain is -$1 per ticket.

misconceptions.A: Forgets to subtract the ticket price.
misconceptions.C: Uses the winning outcome alone and ignores its probability.
misconceptions.D: Assumes a fair game; the price exceeds the expected payout.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A 95 percent confidence interval (the classical, frequentist kind) for a mean is [4.1, 5.3]. Which statement is correct?

options.A: 95 percent of individual observations fall between 4.1 and 5.3.
options.B: If the study were repeated many times, about 95 percent of the intervals built this way would contain the true mean.
options.C: Given this one interval, the probability is 0.95 that the true mean lies inside it.
options.D: The sample mean is between 4.1 and 5.3 with probability 0.95.

recall_items.explanation: The 95 percent describes the long-run behavior of the procedure across repeated samples. Any single interval either contains the true mean or does not.

misconceptions.A: Confuses an interval for the mean with a range for individual values.
misconceptions.C: Treats the fixed true mean as random; that reading belongs to a Bayesian credible interval.
misconceptions.D: The sample mean is a known number that sits at the interval's center.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A p-value of 0.03 in a two-sided test means:

options.A: There is a 3 percent chance the null hypothesis is true.
options.B: If the null hypothesis were true, data at least this extreme would appear about 3 percent of the time.
options.D: There is a 97 percent chance the alternative is true.

recall_items.explanation: A p-value is a statement about the data under the null, not about the probability of either hypothesis, and it says nothing about effect size.

misconceptions.A: Inverts the conditional: p is about data given the null, not the null given data.
misconceptions.C: Small p can come from a tiny effect in a huge sample.
misconceptions.D: Same inversion as A, with 1 minus p.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: An analyst tests 40 product features for an effect on retention at the 5 percent level and finds 2 significant. What is the best reading of this result?

options.A: Two features clearly work.
options.B: With 40 tests and no real effects, about 2 false positives are expected by chance.
options.D: The other 38 features hurt retention.

recall_items.explanation: At a 5 percent threshold, 40 null tests produce 2 false positives on average. Two hits is exactly the chance expectation, so a correction for multiple comparisons or a replication is needed before believing them.

misconceptions.A: Ignores the multiple-comparisons problem.
misconceptions.C: Sample size affects power, not the false-positive rate.
misconceptions.D: Non-significance says nothing about harm.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: You want to know whether the average session length differs between users on two app versions, with 500 users each and no pairing between groups. Which test fits?

options.A: Paired t-test
options.B: Two-sample (independent) t-test
options.D: One-sample t-test against zero

recall_items.explanation: Two independent groups and a continuous outcome call for an independent-samples t-test (or its non-parametric cousin if lengths are heavily skewed).

misconceptions.A: Pairing requires the same units measured twice.
misconceptions.C: Chi-squared is for counts in categories, not a continuous mean.
misconceptions.D: Comparing one mean to zero does not compare the two versions.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A linear regression of monthly spend on age and income gives: age coefficient 2.5 (p = 0.001), income coefficient 0.02 (p < 0.001). How do you read the age coefficient?

options.A: Each extra year of age is associated with 2.5 more spend, holding income fixed.
options.B: Age causes spend to rise by 2.5 per year.
options.C: Age explains 2.5 percent of the variance in spend.
options.D: Spend rises 2.5 times for each year of age.

recall_items.explanation: A coefficient in multiple regression is the association with the outcome holding the other predictors constant. It is additive, not multiplicative, and not causal on its own.

misconceptions.B: Observational regression shows association; causation needs a design that rules out confounding.
misconceptions.C: Variance explained is R-squared, not a coefficient.
misconceptions.D: A linear coefficient is additive; a multiplicative reading belongs to a log-outcome model.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Which plot is the standard first check for whether a linear model's errors have constant variance?

options.A: Residuals against fitted values
options.B: Histogram of the outcome
options.D: Correlation matrix of predictors

recall_items.explanation: A funnel shape in residuals versus fitted values signals non-constant variance (heteroscedasticity). A flat band is what you want.

misconceptions.B: The outcome's shape is not the error's shape.
misconceptions.C: Useful for autocorrelation in time series, not variance.
misconceptions.D: Shows collinearity among predictors, a different assumption.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Adding an L2 (ridge) penalty to a regression mainly does what?

options.A: Sets most coefficients exactly to zero.
options.B: Shrinks coefficients toward zero to reduce variance, at the cost of some bias.
options.D: Makes the model fit the training data better.

recall_items.explanation: Ridge trades a little bias for lower variance by shrinking coefficients, which usually improves out-of-sample error when predictors are many or correlated.

misconceptions.A: Exact zeros are the L1 (lasso) behavior.
misconceptions.C: The intercept is normally left unpenalized.
misconceptions.D: A penalty makes training fit worse by design; the gain is on new data.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A logistic regression for churn gives a coefficient of 0.69 on 'had a support ticket'. The odds ratio is about 2. What does this mean?

options.A: Customers with a ticket are twice as likely to churn in probability terms, whatever the baseline.
options.B: The odds of churn are about twice as high for customers with a ticket, holding other predictors fixed.
options.D: A ticket adds 0.69 to the churn probability.

recall_items.explanation: Logistic coefficients are log-odds; exp(0.69) is about 2, so the odds double. The change in probability depends on the baseline rate.

misconceptions.A: Doubling odds is not doubling probability unless the baseline is small.
misconceptions.C: A coefficient is not a rate.
misconceptions.D: Coefficients are on the log-odds scale, not the probability scale.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Cities with more ice cream sales have more drownings. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Ice cream causes drowning.
options.B: A common cause, hot weather, raises both.
options.D: It is a coincidence in every city.

recall_items.explanation: A confounder (temperature) drives both variables. Conditioning on it removes the association.

misconceptions.A: Mistakes correlation for causation.
misconceptions.C: Reverse causation is possible in principle but implausible here.
misconceptions.D: A consistent pattern across cities is not a coincidence; it has a cause.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Why does random assignment in an experiment allow a causal reading of the difference between groups?

options.A: It makes the sample larger.
options.B: It balances both measured and unmeasured confounders between groups in expectation.
options.D: It guarantees the groups are identical.

recall_items.explanation: Randomization breaks the link between treatment and every other cause of the outcome, known or unknown, so the groups differ only by chance and by treatment.

misconceptions.A: Sample size affects precision, not confounding.
misconceptions.C: Measurement error is a separate problem.
misconceptions.D: Groups still differ by chance; randomization makes those differences unsystematic.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A company rolled out a new onboarding flow in March. You have monthly retention for this company and for five similar companies that did not change anything. Which design fits best?

options.A: Before-after comparison of this company alone
options.B: Difference-in-differences using the other companies as the comparison trend
options.C: A simple correlation of onboarding and retention
options.D: A randomized A/B test on the already-collected data

recall_items.explanation: Difference-in-differences uses the comparison companies to estimate what would have happened without the change, under a parallel-trends assumption.

misconceptions.A: Ignores anything else that changed in March, such as seasonality.
misconceptions.C: A correlation cannot separate the rollout from other changes.
misconceptions.D: Randomization has to happen before the data are collected.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: In a causal diagram, you want the effect of X on Y. Z is caused by both X and Y (a collider). What happens if you control for Z?

options.A: Nothing; controlling for more variables is always safer.
options.B: You open a spurious path and bias the estimate.
options.D: You increase the sample size.

recall_items.explanation: Conditioning on a collider creates an association between its causes that was not there before. The rule is to control for confounders, never colliders.

misconceptions.A: More controls can add bias when one is a collider or a mediator.
misconceptions.C: Z is not a confounder; it sits downstream of X and Y.
misconceptions.D: Controlling for a variable does not change the sample size.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A model scores 99 percent on training data and 71 percent on new data. The most likely issue is:

options.A: Underfitting
options.B: Overfitting
options.D: The model needs more parameters

recall_items.explanation: A large gap between training and held-out performance is the signature of overfitting: the model memorized noise in the training set.

misconceptions.A: Underfitting would show poor performance on both sets.
misconceptions.C: Blaming new data skips the diagnosis.
misconceptions.D: More parameters widen the gap.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: What is the purpose of k-fold cross-validation?

options.A: To train the model k times faster.
options.B: To estimate out-of-sample performance using all the data for both training and validation across folds.
options.D: To increase the training set size by k.

recall_items.explanation: Each fold is held out once while the others train, which gives a more stable estimate of generalization than a single split.

misconceptions.A: It costs k times more training, not less.
misconceptions.C: Cross-validation does not alter the data.
misconceptions.D: The data size is fixed; folds rotate which part is held out.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A fraud dataset has 0.5 percent positives. A model predicts 'not fraud' for everyone. Which statement is true?

options.A: Accuracy is 99.5 percent and the model is useful.
options.B: Accuracy is 99.5 percent, recall on fraud is 0, and the model is useless.
options.D: The model has a high F1 score.

recall_items.explanation: Precision is undefined because the model predicts no positives. On imbalanced classes, accuracy follows the majority class. Recall, precision, and the precision-recall curve are the metrics that matter here.

misconceptions.A: High accuracy hides zero fraud caught.
misconceptions.C: Precision is undefined when no positives are predicted.
misconceptions.D: F1 is zero when recall is zero.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Why does a random forest usually generalize better than a single deep decision tree?

options.A: It uses fewer features.
options.B: Averaging many trees trained on bootstrapped samples and random feature subsets lowers variance.
options.D: It fits the training data more exactly.

recall_items.explanation: Single deep trees have high variance. Bagging and feature randomness make the trees' errors less correlated, so their average is more stable.

misconceptions.A: Each split considers a random subset, but the forest uses all features overall.
misconceptions.C: Depth is similar; the gain comes from averaging.
misconceptions.D: A forest usually fits training data slightly less exactly than one unpruned tree.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: In Bayesian inference, the posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the ______.

options.A: prior
options.B: p-value
options.D: evidence

recall_items.explanation: Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. The evidence (marginal likelihood) is the normalizing constant in the denominator.

misconceptions.C: Sample size enters through the likelihood, not as a separate factor.
misconceptions.D: The evidence divides, it does not multiply.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A hierarchical model estimates a per-school effect with partial pooling. A school with 5 students has a raw mean far above the others. What does the model do to its estimate?

options.A: Leaves it at the raw mean.
options.B: Shrinks it toward the overall mean, more than it would for a school with 500 students.
options.C: Sets it to the overall mean exactly.
options.D: Drops the school.

recall_items.explanation: Partial pooling shrinks noisy small-group estimates toward the population mean in proportion to their uncertainty. Large groups move little.

misconceptions.A: No pooling would leave it; partial pooling shrinks.
misconceptions.C: Complete pooling would do that; partial pooling keeps some of the school's signal.
misconceptions.D: Small groups are kept and regularized, not removed.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: After MCMC sampling, a parameter shows R-hat of 1.21. What should you do?

options.A: Report the estimate; 1.21 is close to 1.
options.B: Treat the chains as not converged: run longer, check for multimodality or reparameterize.
options.D: Increase the prior variance.

recall_items.explanation: R-hat compares between-chain and within-chain variance; values above about 1.01 mean the chains disagree, so the posterior summary is not trustworthy yet.

misconceptions.A: The common threshold is 1.01; 1.21 is far from it.
misconceptions.C: Removing a chain hides the problem.
misconceptions.D: Prior variance is a modeling choice, not a convergence fix.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A 95 percent Bayesian credible interval for an effect is [0.2, 0.9]. Which reading is correct?

options.A: Given the model and data, there is a 95 percent probability the effect lies between 0.2 and 0.9.
options.B: 95 percent of repeated samples would give an effect in this range.
options.D: The p-value is 0.05.

recall_items.explanation: A credible interval is a direct probability statement about the parameter, conditional on the prior and the data. That is the reading a confidence interval does not allow.

misconceptions.B: Repeated-sampling coverage is the confidence-interval reading.
misconceptions.C: The interval expresses uncertainty; the midpoint is one summary of it.
misconceptions.D: Credible intervals do not come with p-values.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: This should print the average order total per city but prints a method object. Fix it.
recall_items.code:
df["total"] = df["price"] * df["qty"]
result = df.groupby("city")["total"].mean
print(result)

options.A: Change .mean to .mean()
options.B: Change groupby to sort_values
options.D: Replace print with return

recall_items.explanation: Without parentheses, .mean is a reference to the method, not a call. Adding () runs the aggregation.

misconceptions.C: Selecting the column is correct; the missing call is the bug.
misconceptions.D: return outside a function raises an error and does not fix the bug.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: What does this query return?
recall_items.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS n_orders
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

options.A: Every customer, with order counts and 0 for customers with no orders.
options.B: Only customers who have at least one order, with their order counts.
options.C: Every order with the customer's name repeated.
options.D: An error, because COUNT needs a WHERE clause.

recall_items.explanation: An inner JOIN keeps only customers with a matching order row. Customers with no orders are absent; a LEFT JOIN would keep them with a count of 0.

misconceptions.A: That is the LEFT JOIN result, with COUNT(o.id) for the zeros.
misconceptions.C: GROUP BY collapses the rows to one per customer.
misconceptions.D: COUNT works without WHERE.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: This filter should keep rows where status is 'active' AND age is over 30, but raises a ValueError about ambiguous truth values. Fix it.

options.A: Wrap each condition in parentheses and use & instead of and
options.B: Replace > with >=
options.D: Convert age to a string first

recall_items.explanation: pandas needs element-wise operators (&, |) and parentheses, because the Python keyword and tries to evaluate a whole Series as one boolean.

misconceptions.B: The comparison operator is not the problem.
misconceptions.C: df.query works, but the condition needs quotes around 'active'.
misconceptions.D: Comparing strings to 30 breaks the filter.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A teammate cannot reproduce your notebook's numbers. The most common cause from this list is:

options.A: Cells were run out of order, so the state depends on the run history.
options.B: Their laptop is slower.
options.C: pandas rounds differently on other machines.
options.D: Notebooks cannot be shared.

recall_items.explanation: Notebook state is whatever ran last, in whatever order. Restart the kernel and run all cells top to bottom before sharing, and pin package versions.

misconceptions.C: Same version, same arithmetic.
misconceptions.D: Notebooks share fine when they run clean from the top.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: Which opening line fits a one-paragraph findings summary for a product manager?

options.A: We ran a logistic regression with L2 regularization on 14 features.
options.B: The new checkout page showed an estimated lift of about 0.5 points in conversion, with an interval that includes zero; we recommend extending the test two weeks.
options.C: Data was collected between March and May.
options.D: Please see the attached notebook.

recall_items.explanation: Lead with the finding, its uncertainty, and the recommendation. Method and data details come after, for readers who want them.

misconceptions.A: Opens with method; the reader wants the result.
misconceptions.C: Opens with logistics, not the answer.
misconceptions.D: Pushes the work onto the reader.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A stakeholder asks: 'So is the effect real or not?' Your interval is [-0.1, 1.2] points. The best answer is:

options.A: No, it is not significant, so there is no effect.
options.B: The best estimate is a lift of about 0.5 points, and the data are consistent with anything from a slight loss to a 1.2-point gain. If a wrong call is cheap, ship and monitor; if it is costly, run the test longer.
options.D: Statistics cannot answer that.

recall_items.explanation: Translate the interval into the decision's terms: the point estimate, the range, and what the uncertainty means for the choice in front of them.

misconceptions.A: Non-significant is not 'no effect'.
misconceptions.C: Drops the uncertainty the stakeholder needs.
misconceptions.D: Statistics does answer it, with a range and a recommendation.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: A dashboard for weekly executives should show:

options.A: Every metric the team tracks, on one page.
options.B: The 3 to 5 metrics tied to decisions they make, each with its target and trend.
options.C: Raw tables so they can compute their own numbers.
options.D: Only the metrics that improved this week.

recall_items.explanation: A dashboard serves decisions. Few metrics, each with a target and a trend, is what gets read and acted on.

misconceptions.A: Everything on one page means nothing stands out.
misconceptions.C: Executives want answers, not homework.
misconceptions.D: Hiding declines removes the information decisions need most.

recall_items.author: hand

recall_items.stem: You must report that the model's forecast error doubled last month. Which phrasing is both honest and useful?

options.A: The model is broken.
options.B: Forecast error rose from 4 to 8 percent in September; the jump coincides with the pricing change, and we are retraining with the new price data this week.
options.C: There were some fluctuations in performance.
options.D: Error went up but it is probably fine.

recall_items.explanation: State the number, the likely cause, and the action. That is what a reader needs to trust the report and to decide whether to intervene.

misconceptions.A: Alarms without a number or a cause.
misconceptions.C: Vague enough to hide a real problem.
misconceptions.D: Dismisses a doubling without evidence.

recall_items.author: hand

scenarios.title: Ship the checkout page?
scenarios.context: Your manager shares an A/B test of a new checkout page. The old page converted 4.1 percent and the new page 4.6 percent, with 10,000 users in each group. The two-sided p-value is 0.08. She wants to ship the new page today.

steps.prompt: What do you tell her about the result?

options.A: The new page raises conversion by 0.5 points; ship it.
options.B: There is a 92 percent chance the new page is better.
options.C: The result is inconclusive at the 5 percent level. The lift could be anywhere from slightly negative to about 1 point. Extend the test, or decide based on the cost of a wrong call.
options.D: The test failed, so the two pages perform the same.

steps.explanation: The 95 percent interval for the difference runs from about -0.07 to 1.07 points, so the data do not settle the question at the 5 percent level, and the right move depends on the cost of being wrong.

misconceptions.A: Treats the observed lift as certain.
misconceptions.B: Reads the p-value as the probability the hypothesis is true.
misconceptions.D: Treats 'not significant' as 'no difference'.

steps.prompt: Nobody knows yet what a wrong call would cost. What should happen next?

options.A: Extend the test for a fixed two more weeks, set now, then decide.
options.B: Ship now, and roll back if conversion drops over the next week.
options.C: Keep the old page and close the test.
options.D: Rerun the analysis with a one-sided test to get p under 0.05.

steps.explanation: Extending the test for a period fixed in advance is the default when the cost of a wrong call is unknown; stopping the moment the interval clears zero would inflate false positives. B is defensible when shipping is cheap to reverse and the downside is small. C discards a likely positive effect. D changes the test after seeing the data, which inflates false positives.

misconceptions.B: Defensible only when rollback is cheap and the downside is small; say that out loud if you pick it.
misconceptions.C: Throws away a result whose best estimate is positive.
misconceptions.D: Choosing the test after seeing the data is p-hacking.

steps.prompt: In one or two lines, explain the decision to your manager.
steps.model_answer: The new page probably helps, but the test cannot yet rule out no effect. Two more weeks of data would make the call clear; if we must decide today, the downside is small and we can ship with monitoring.
checkpoints: States the best estimate and that the interval includes zero
Ties the recommendation to the cost of a wrong call
Gives a concrete next step with a time or condition

scenarios.title: Revenue looks too good
scenarios.context: The monthly revenue dashboard shows September revenue up 38 percent, which nobody expected. You check the pipeline: the orders table is joined to a shipments table before summing order totals, and some orders ship in several packages.

steps.prompt: What is the most likely cause of the jump?

options.A: Sales really rose 38 percent.
options.B: Orders with several shipments appear several times after the join, so their totals are summed more than once.
options.D: The dashboard caches old data.

steps.explanation: A one-to-many join on orders to shipments duplicates each multi-package order once per package. Summing order totals afterward counts those orders several times. September likely had more split shipments.

misconceptions.A: An unexplained 38 percent jump that coincides with a pipeline detail deserves a check before it is believed.
misconceptions.C: A currency change would shift every month, not one.
misconceptions.D: Caching shows old numbers, not inflated ones.

options.A: Compare the row count after the join with the number of distinct order ids, and compare the summed total with a sum computed on the orders table alone.
options.B: Tell leadership that revenue is up 38 percent.
options.D: Divide September revenue by 1.38.

steps.explanation: Verify the diagnosis by comparing rows to distinct orders and checking a reference sum before touching the pipeline or the message. The fix is to aggregate shipments per order before the join, or sum on the orders table.

misconceptions.B: Reporting an unverified number is the costly mistake here.
misconceptions.C: The table is fine; the join order is the bug.
misconceptions.D: Guessing a correction factor hides the real error.

steps.prompt: Write the one-line note you would post in the team channel.
steps.model_answer: September revenue on the dashboard is inflated: the shipments join duplicates multi-package orders before the sum. Verified by comparing joined rows to distinct orders. Fix in review; corrected figure by end of day.
checkpoints: Names the cause (duplicate rows from the join) and the effect (inflated sum)
Gives the fix and when the corrected number arrives

scenarios.title: The churn model is too perfect
scenarios.context: A colleague built a churn model that scores 99 percent accuracy on the validation set. One of the features is 'days since last login', computed at the end of the data window. Churned customers stop logging in by definition.

options.A: The model is excellent and should go to production.
options.B: The feature leaks the label: it is computed after churn happens, so it encodes the answer.
options.C: The validation set is too small.
options.D: Accuracy is the wrong metric, so the model is actually bad.

steps.explanation: Days since last login measured at the end of the window is large for every churned customer, because churn means they stopped logging in. The feature is a consequence of the label, not a predictor available at decision time.

misconceptions.A: Near-perfect scores on a hard problem are a warning sign, not a success.
misconceptions.C: Sample size does not create leakage.
misconceptions.D: Metric choice matters, but the number here comes from leakage.

options.A: Compute every feature as of a cutoff date before the churn window, and evaluate on customers whose churn status is observed after that date.
options.B: Remove the feature and keep everything else as is.
options.D: Add more features.

steps.explanation: The fix is temporal: features must use only information available at the moment the prediction would be made. Removing one feature leaves any other leaking feature in place.

misconceptions.B: Other features computed at the end of the window may leak too.
misconceptions.C: Changing the metric does not stop the leak.
misconceptions.D: More features built the same way add more leakage.

steps.prompt: Explain to your colleague in one or two lines why the 99 percent is not real.
steps.model_answer: The model is reading the answer off the feature: days since last login is computed after the customer already churned. Rebuilding features as of a cutoff date will give a lower but honest score.
checkpoints: Identifies the feature as a consequence of the label
Explains the timing problem (computed after the outcome)
Says what an honest evaluation looks like
